title: The reports, reviewed

cards: A message lands in a family group chat late at night. It begins, the Prophet said, then a beautiful sentence, then a row of heart emojis. Somebody's aunt has already forwarded it to her other groups.
Nobody asks where it came from. This year spent a long stretch on exactly that question.

Before a sentence could be called a hadith, scholars wanted to know who said it, who heard it, who passed it on, and whether every one of those people could be trusted. Today, how a hadith reaches you.

teach.b: A hadith is a report of what the Prophet, peace be upon him, said, did, or approved. Every hadith has two halves: a chain, the isnad, and a text, the matn.
The chain is the list of people: I heard it from this one, who heard it from that one, all the way back. Why did the chain matter so much?

teach.h: WITHOUT THE CHAIN, ANYONE SAYS ANYTHING.
teach.b: In the introduction to Sahih Muslim, a saying is recorded from the early scholar Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak, in paraphrase: the chain is part of the religion, and without it anyone could say whatever they liked.
The forwarded message problem, named long before phones. How was it tested?
Scholars wrote about the narrators themselves, the science the year called rijal: was this man truthful, was his memory sharp, did he really meet the one he quoted?
They tested the text too, asking whether it fit the Qur'an and the known sunnah.
Then they graded: sahih, sound; hasan, good; da'if, weak; and some reports were exposed as fabricated.
And the people who carried it. Students traveled to hear a report from its source, and memorized chains by heart.
Women carried it too, from Aisha onward, and the year met Karimah al-Marwaziyyah, who taught Bukhari's Sahih.
The same introduction to Sahih Muslim carries a warning, in paraphrase: it is enough of a lie for a person to pass on everything they hear. That sentence could sit above every share button.

how: Muslims read hadith in collections such as Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, and Shia Muslims in their own collections such as al-Kafi; scholars grade each report by its chain and its text, and teachers often give the source and grade when they quote one.

o: what the Prophet said, did or approved, each with a tested chain
stories about the companions written down by historians

games.q: a beautiful saying lands in your group chat: "the Prophet said…" no source. what would the hadith scholars do?
o: forward it fast; it sounds good.
ask who narrated it and whether the chain and text hold up.
games.why: they asked for the chain. a saying in Sahih Muslim's introduction puts it this way: without the chain, anyone could say whatever they liked.

practice: Bring to mind one hadith you met this year whose source you actually know: actions are by intentions, from Bukhari, or none of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself, also Bukhari.
Hold its words for a few breaths, and think of one person who might be glad to hear it, with its source attached, the way the scholars would have wanted.

wordCard.voice: The reports. Hadith: what the Prophet said, did, or approved, each carried by a chain of named people and tested before it was trusted. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the chain of narrators that carries a report back to its source.

carryVoice: Your line: the chain holds. It holds because people checked it, link by link. See you tomorrow.
